item.title: AST-grep Rewrote Tree-sitter in Rust: 30% Faster Code Analysis for AI Tools
item.description: AST-grep rewrote Tree-sitter's C core in Rust using ChatGPT, achieving 29.74% faster parsing and 22.2% faster end-to-end code analysis for AI tools.
item.content:encoded:
What Is the AST-grep Tree-sitter Rust Rewrite?

AST-grep, the popular structural code search tool with over 15,000 GitHub stars, rewrote Tree-sitter’s C parsing core entirely in Rust using ChatGPT-assisted code generation. The result is a 29.74% improvement in raw parsing throughput and a 22.2% faster end-to-end code analysis pipeline, making it significantly faster for AI coding agents and developer tools that rely on syntax-tree-based code understanding.

Why Did AST-grep Rewrite Tree-sitter in Rust?

Tree-sitter has been the gold standard for incremental parsing in code editors since its release. Its C core is battle-tested and powers syntax highlighting in editors like Neovim, VS Code, and Zed. But AST-grep’s use case is fundamentally different from an editor’s.

The Problem with Tree-sitter’s C Core for AI Workloads

Tree-sitter was designed for interactive editing, where incremental parsing — reusing the old syntax tree after small edits — is critical. AI coding agents, however, don’t edit files character by character. They analyze entire codebases at once, searching for structural patterns across thousands of files. For this workload, incremental parsing is unnecessary overhead.

The C codebase also presented maintenance challenges. AST-grep is written in Rust, and maintaining a C foreign-function interface (FFI) to Tree-sitter introduced complexity, build friction, and limited optimization opportunities. By rewriting the parser in Rust, the team could eliminate the FFI boundary, remove features irrelevant to AI workloads, and apply Rust-specific optimizations like arena allocation.

Removing Incremental Parsing: A Feature, Not a Bug

The most controversial decision in the rewrite was removing incremental old-tree reuse — a core Tree-sitter feature. For AI agent workloads that parse fresh code on every invocation, this feature was pure overhead. The Rust rewrite simply skips it, which simplifies the parser and contributes directly to the performance gains.

How Did ChatGPT Assist in Writing the Rust Parser?

One of the most remarkable aspects of this project is that ChatGPT generated the majority of the Rust code. The AST-grep team used the AI model as a code generation engine, translating Tree-sitter’s C parsing logic into idiomatic Rust.

The AI-Assisted Rewrite Workflow

The team fed Tree-sitter’s C source code to ChatGPT and asked it to produce equivalent Rust implementations. The AI handled the mechanical translation — converting C’s manual memory management to Rust’s ownership model, translating pointer arithmetic to safe Rust patterns, and restructuring C macros into Rust generics and traits.

However, the AI-generated code was not production-ready out of the box. The team described a “load-bearing wall” metaphor: AI made the rewrite possible by handling the bulk translation, but human expertise in profiling, benchmarking, and iterative optimization turned the translated code into a high-performance parser. The AI wrote the first draft; humans made it fast.

What This Means for Systems Programming

This project demonstrates a new paradigm for systems-level rewrites. Traditionally, porting a mature C codebase to Rust requires months of manual effort. With AI-assisted code generation, the mechanical translation phase is dramatically compressed. The human effort shifts from “writing code” to “directing, profiling, and optimizing” — a fundamentally different skill set that combines domain expertise with AI orchestration.

What Performance Gains Did the Rust Rewrite Achieve?

The rewrite was benchmarked extensively, and the results are documented across a four-part blog series. Here are the key numbers:

Metric C Baseline Rust Rewrite Improvement
Raw parsing throughput Baseline +29.74% 29.74% faster
Tree traversal throughput Baseline +10.16% 10.16% faster
End-to-end ast-grep outline (user CPU) 1.233s 0.960s 22.2% faster
Memory usage (RSS, ast-grep run) 26.52 MiB 34.43 MiB +29.8% more memory
TypeScript stress corpus peak >1 GiB 91.2 MiB ~91% reduction

Raw Parsing: The Headline 30% Gain

The raw parsing throughput improvement of 29.74% is the headline number. This measures how fast the parser can produce a syntax tree from source code, isolated from any application logic. The gain comes from several Rust-specific optimizations:

  • Arena allocation: Instead of individual heap allocations for each syntax node, the Rust parser uses arena allocators that batch memory in contiguous blocks. This reduces allocation overhead and improves cache locality.
  • Compact indexes: The Rust version uses smaller, more cache-friendly data structures for internal node representations.
  • Eliminated FFI overhead: Without the C-to-Rust FFI boundary, function calls that previously crossed the language barrier are now direct Rust calls.

End-to-End Performance: The Real-World Number

While the raw parser is 30% faster, the end-to-end ast-grep outline command — a realistic workload that parses code and extracts structural information — improved by 22.2% (0.960s vs 1.233s user CPU time). The gap between 30% and 22% is instructive: parser speed is only one component of total application performance. Other factors like I/O, tree traversal, and pattern matching also contribute to wall-clock time.

How Did GLR Optimization Contribute to the Speedup?

Tree-sitter uses a Generalized LR (GLR) parsing algorithm, which can handle ambiguous grammars by maintaining a graph of possible parse states rather than a single stack. This is what makes Tree-sitter so robust for real-world code — it can parse incomplete or syntactically incorrect files that would choke a standard LR parser.

The 99% Optimization Insight

During the rewrite, the AST-grep team made a critical observation: in real-world code analysis workloads, 99% of the parser stack follows a single straight path. The GLR graph — with its branching and merging — is rarely needed. This insight drove a key optimization: optimize for the common case (single-path parsing) and fall back to the full GLR machinery only when ambiguity is detected.

This is a textbook example of profile-driven optimization. Rather than optimizing the GLR algorithm in the abstract, the team measured actual workloads and discovered that the theoretical worst case (massive ambiguity) is practically nonexistent for the codebases AST-grep analyzes.

Memory Layout and Arena Allocation

The Rust rewrite introduced arena-based memory management for syntax nodes. Instead of allocating each node individually on the heap — which causes fragmentation and poor cache behavior — the parser allocates nodes in contiguous memory regions. This has two benefits:

  1. Faster allocation and deallocation: Arena allocation is essentially a bump-pointer operation, far cheaper than individual malloc/free cycles.
  2. Better cache locality: Contiguous nodes are more likely to be in the CPU cache together, speeding up tree traversal.

The memory tradeoff is real: RSS increased by 29.8% (34.43 MiB vs 26.52 MiB) in the ast-grep benchmark. However, the TypeScript stress corpus tells a different story. Before optimization, peak memory exceeded 1 GiB. After arena optimization, it dropped to 91.2 MiB — a 91% reduction. The arena allocator prevents memory fragmentation that previously caused exponential growth on large files.

What Is the Gap Between Parser Benchmarks and Application Performance?

This is one of the most important lessons from the rewrite. The raw parser benchmark shows a 30% improvement, but the end-to-end application only sees 22%. Why the gap?

The Components of End-to-End Performance

An ast-grep command involves several stages:

  1. File I/O: Reading source files from disk
  2. Parsing: Building syntax trees (the 30% faster part)
  3. Tree traversal: Walking the syntax tree to find matches
  4. Pattern matching: Applying the user’s search pattern
  5. Output formatting: Displaying results

Only step 2 benefits from the parser rewrite. Steps 1, 3, 4, and 5 are unchanged. The 22.2% end-to-end improvement is actually quite impressive when you consider that parsing is only one component of the pipeline.

The Initial Performance Regression

Interestingly, the first version of the Rust rewrite was actually slower than the C baseline. The AI-generated code, while functionally correct, lacked the optimizations that years of C development had accumulated. Only after profiling and iterative tuning — arena allocation, compact indexes, GLR optimization — did the Rust version surpass the C baseline.

This is a crucial lesson for anyone considering AI-assisted rewrites: the AI can generate correct code quickly, but making it fast requires the same profiling and optimization skills that traditional performance engineering demands.

What Lessons Does This Project Offer for AI-Assisted Systems Programming?

The AST-grep Tree-sitter rewrite is a case study in the future of systems programming. Here are the key takeaways:

AI as a Force Multiplier, Not a Replacement

ChatGPT wrote the bulk of the Rust code, but human engineers directed the effort, profiled the results, and iterated on performance. The AI compressed the translation phase from months to weeks, but the optimization phase still required deep expertise in parsing algorithms, memory management, and Rust’s performance characteristics.

Profile Before You Optimize

The 99% single-path GLR insight came from profiling real workloads, not from theoretical analysis. The team didn’t guess where the bottlenecks were — they measured them. This principle applies to any performance optimization project: measure first, optimize second.

Removing Features Is a Legitimate Optimization

The decision to remove incremental parsing and native Wasm grammar loading was controversial but correct for AST-grep’s use case. Not every feature from the original codebase needs to survive a rewrite. Understanding which features are “load-bearing” for your specific workload and which are dead weight is a critical skill.

Rust’s Ownership Model Pays Off

The Rust rewrite eliminated an entire class of memory bugs that plague C codebases. While the C version of Tree-sitter is battle-tested, the Rust version gains compile-time memory safety guarantees. For a parser that processes untrusted source code, this is a significant security advantage.

How Does This Impact AI Coding Tools and the Ecosystem?

The implications extend far beyond AST-grep itself. Tree-sitter is the backbone of code analysis for many AI coding tools, including:

  • CodeRabbit: Uses AST-grep for AI-native code review and linting, combining structural search with LLM analysis for code quality at scale.
  • CodeRLM: A Tree-sitter-backed code indexing system for LLM agents that improves code understanding through syntax-tree-aware indexing.
  • VT Code: An AST-aware Rust TUI coding agent that integrates both Tree-sitter and AST-grep for terminal-based AI coding.

Faster Code Analysis for Agentic Workflows

AI coding agents analyze entire codebases to understand context before generating code. A 22% faster end-to-end analysis means agents can process more code in less time, leading to better context understanding and more accurate code generation. For agentic workflows that parse thousands of files per session, this performance improvement compounds significantly.

The Growing Tree-sitter Ecosystem

The Tree-sitter ecosystem is expanding rapidly. The Rust rewrite repo itself has already attracted attention, and the broader community is watching closely. If the Rust version proves stable and performant, it could become the foundation for a new generation of Rust-native code analysis tools.

What This Means for Developer Tooling

Faster parsing means faster IDE features, faster linting, faster code search, and faster AI code generation. Every tool that depends on syntax-tree analysis benefits from a faster Tree-sitter. The Rust rewrite doesn’t just make AST-grep faster — it raises the performance ceiling for the entire ecosystem of tools built on Tree-sitter.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Rust rewrite of Tree-sitter a drop-in replacement for the C version?

No. The Rust rewrite removes incremental parsing and native Wasm grammar loading, which are features designed for interactive editing. It is optimized for AI agent workloads and batch code analysis, not for use as an editor plugin. If you need incremental parsing for an editor, the C version remains the right choice.

How much faster is the Rust version in real-world use?

End-to-end ast-grep commands run approximately 22% faster in user CPU time. Raw parsing is 30% faster. The exact improvement depends on your workload — codebases with many large files benefit more than those with many small files, where I/O overhead dominates.

Did ChatGPT write all the Rust code?

ChatGPT generated the initial translation from C to Rust, but the team performed extensive profiling and optimization to achieve the performance gains. The AI handled the mechanical translation; humans optimized the result. The final code is a collaboration between AI generation and human performance engineering.

Does the Rust rewrite use more memory?

In typical workloads, the Rust version uses about 29.8% more RSS (34.43 MiB vs 26.52 MiB). However, for large files, the arena allocator prevents memory fragmentation, resulting in dramatically lower peak memory — 91.2 MiB vs over 1 GiB for the C version on a TypeScript stress corpus.

Will the Rust rewrite replace the C version of Tree-sitter?

For AST-grep’s use case, yes. For the broader Tree-sitter ecosystem, it depends on whether the community adopts the Rust version for editor integration. The C version remains the standard for interactive editing due to its incremental parsing support. The two versions may coexist for different use cases.

item.title: AI Coding Agents Are Removing Programming Language Barriers in 2026
item.description: AI coding agents like Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot are removing programming language barriers, enabling developers to work across languages they never learned.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — The End of Language-Specific Developers

AI coding agents are removing programming language barriers by acting as intelligent pairing partners that handle syntax, standard library patterns, and common idioms across virtually every language. Developers who once specialized in a single language can now contribute meaningfully to C++, Rust, Go, Python, and JavaScript projects from day one, using tools like Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot to bridge the gap between what they know and what the codebase requires.

What Are AI Coding Agents?

AI coding agents are the next evolution of code assistants. Unlike traditional autocomplete tools that suggest the next line, AI coding agents operate as autonomous or semi-autonomous programming partners. They can understand a full codebase context, plan multi-file changes, execute refactors, run tests, and iterate on feedback — all while handling the mechanical details of language syntax and standard library usage.

The three leading tools in this space are:

  • Cursor — An AI-native IDE that combines agentic workflows with deep codebase understanding, semantic search, and multi-agent collaboration features.
  • Claude Code — Anthropic’s terminal-based agentic coding tool that handles complex multi-file edits, git operations, and autonomous code generation across languages.
  • GitHub Copilot — The most widely adopted AI code assistant, recognized as a Leader in Gartner’s Magic Quadrant for AI Code Assistants for two consecutive years, now evolving from autocomplete to full agentic workflows.

These tools share a common capability: they abstract away the language-specific knowledge that previously required months or years of dedicated study.

The Rails at Scale Story — From Ruby-Only to Multi-Language in One Year

The most compelling real-world example comes from Stan Lo, a member of Shopify’s Ruby DX team. Writing on the Rails at Scale blog, Lo described how he went from being a Ruby-only developer to contributing meaningfully in C++, C, and Rust within a single year — all because of AI coding tools.

Lo’s experience is not an outlier. He used Cursor and Claude Code as complementary pairing partners, not as code generators that he blindly accepted. The AI handled syntax, standard patterns, and general programming concepts while Lo provided project-specific context, requirements, and critical judgment. This pairing model allowed him to be productive in unfamiliar languages from day one, learning the language’s deeper idioms and conventions organically through the process of building real software.

This story illustrates a fundamental shift: the barrier to contributing in a new programming language is no longer measured in months of study. It is measured in hours of AI-assisted onboarding.

How AI Coding Agents Remove Language Barriers

Syntax and Pattern Offloading

Every programming language has a syntax that must be memorized, a standard library that must be learned, and common patterns that must be internalized. For a developer switching languages, this cognitive load is enormous. AI coding agents absorb this burden entirely.

When a developer types a prompt like “parse this JSON config file and validate each field,” the AI agent knows how to do this in Python (using json.loads and a schema library), in Rust (using serde_json with serde::Deserialize), in Go (using encoding/json with struct tags), or in JavaScript (using JSON.parse with a validation library). The developer does not need to know the specific API calls — they only need to describe the intent.

Real-Time Learning While Building

The traditional model of learning a programming language follows a rigid sequence: study syntax, learn the standard library, build small projects, then graduate to production code. AI coding agents invert this model. Developers can start with production work immediately and learn the language as they go.

Each AI-generated code block becomes a learning opportunity. The developer sees idiomatic patterns, standard library usage, and language-specific conventions in real time, within the context of their actual project. This contextual learning is far more effective than abstract tutorials because it is immediately applied and reinforced.

The Complementary Pairing Model

The most effective use of AI coding agents is not as autonomous code generators but as complementary pairing partners. In this model:

Role AI Agent Human Developer
Syntax Handles all language syntax and standard library Provides intent and requirements
Patterns Suggests idiomatic patterns and best practices Evaluates and adapts to project context
Debugging Identifies common errors and suggests fixes Diagnoses logic errors and edge cases
Architecture Proposes implementation approaches Makes final architectural decisions
Learning Demonstrates language features in context Internalizes patterns through review
Security Catches common vulnerabilities Validates security for business logic

This division of labor is the key insight behind the language barrier removal phenomenon. The AI handles the mechanical aspects of programming that are well-documented and pattern-based, while the human handles the aspects that require judgment, domain knowledge, and project-specific understanding.

The Tools Leading the Change

Cursor — Agentic IDE with Multi-Agent Collaboration

Cursor has positioned itself as more than an AI autocomplete tool. It is an AI-native IDE that is investing heavily in agentic capabilities: secure codebase indexing, semantic search, reinforcement learning for code generation quality, and multi-agent collaboration where multiple AI agents can work together on complex tasks.

Cursor’s key differentiator is its deep codebase understanding. It indexes the entire project, understands relationships between files, and can make contextually aware suggestions that span multiple files and modules. For a developer working in an unfamiliar language, this means Cursor can explain how the existing codebase uses the language, what patterns are already established, and how new code should fit in.

Claude Code — Terminal-Based Autonomous Agent

Claude Code, developed by Anthropic, takes a different approach. It is a terminal-based agentic coding tool designed for developers who prefer command-line workflows. Claude Code can handle complex multi-file edits, execute git operations, run tests, and perform autonomous refactoring across programming languages.

What makes Claude Code particularly effective for cross-language work is its ability to understand the full context of a codebase and make coordinated changes across multiple files. A developer can say “migrate this Python module to use async/await patterns” or “convert this JavaScript function to TypeScript with proper types,” and Claude Code handles the entire transformation, including updating dependent files and fixing type errors.

GitHub Copilot — From Autocomplete to Agentic Workflows

GitHub Copilot, now recognized as a Leader in Gartner’s Magic Quadrant for AI Code Assistants for the second consecutive year, is the most widely adopted AI coding tool. Originally launched as an autocomplete tool, Copilot has evolved significantly. It now supports agentic workflows that can plan, execute, and verify code changes across multiple files and languages.

Copilot’s strength lies in its integration with the GitHub ecosystem. It understands pull requests, issues, and code reviews, and can suggest changes that align with the project’s existing patterns. For developers working across languages, Copilot’s broad language support and deep training data make it particularly effective at generating idiomatic code in less common languages.

Real-World Impact and Statistics

The impact of AI coding agents on language barriers is supported by concrete data and industry recognition:

  • Gartner Magic Quadrant: GitHub Copilot was recognized as a Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Code Assistants for the second consecutive year, validating the market’s confidence in AI-assisted development.
  • Developer Productivity Gains: Multiple surveys and reports show significant productivity improvements for developers using AI coding tools, with the most dramatic gains reported when working in unfamiliar languages or codebases.
  • Community Engagement: The Hacker News discussion on AI removing language barriers received 148 points and 176 comments, indicating strong developer interest and engagement with this topic.
  • Market Growth: The AI code assistant market is projected to grow substantially as tools evolve from simple copilots to autonomous coding agents capable of handling complex, multi-language development tasks.
  • Day-One Productivity: Multiple developer reports, including the Rails at Scale case study, confirm that developers can contribute to unfamiliar codebases and languages from their first day on a project when using AI coding agents.

Challenges and Limitations

Project-Specific Knowledge Gaps

AI coding agents excel at general programming knowledge but struggle with project-specific context. Every codebase has unique conventions, architectural decisions, and business logic that the AI cannot fully understand without extensive context. A developer who blindly accepts AI-generated code without understanding the project’s specific constraints will introduce inconsistencies and technical debt.

Quality and Security Risks

AI-generated code can contain subtle bugs, security vulnerabilities, and performance issues that are not immediately obvious. The AI may suggest patterns that are syntactically correct but semantically wrong for the specific use case. This is particularly dangerous when developers lack the language expertise to evaluate the AI’s output critically.

A developer who does not understand Rust’s ownership model, for example, might accept AI-generated code that compiles but has subtle memory management issues. Similarly, AI-generated JavaScript might introduce prototype pollution vulnerabilities or incorrect async handling that a non-expert would miss.

The Irreplaceable Value of Human Expertise

While AI coding agents can handle syntax and standard patterns, they cannot replace deep human expertise in several critical areas:

  • Architectural decisions: AI can suggest implementation approaches, but it cannot evaluate long-term architectural trade-offs or understand business constraints.
  • Debugging complex issues: AI is good at identifying common errors but struggles with novel, project-specific bugs that require deep understanding of the system.
  • Code review and quality judgment: AI can catch style issues and common anti-patterns, but it cannot evaluate whether code is “good” in the context of the project’s specific quality standards.
  • Security and compliance: AI can flag common vulnerabilities but cannot understand the full security implications of code in a specific business or regulatory context.

What This Means for Developers and Companies

For individual developers, the message is clear: specializing in a single language is no longer a career strategy. The developers who will thrive are those who combine deep problem-solving skills with the ability to use AI tools to work across multiple languages and frameworks. The value of a developer is shifting from “what languages do you know?” to “what problems can you solve?”

For companies, the implications are equally significant. Hiring decisions no longer need to be constrained by language requirements. A company building a Rust backend can hire a Python expert who uses AI coding agents to write idiomatic Rust. This dramatically expands the talent pool and reduces the cost and time of onboarding.

The economics of hiring are changing. Companies can now prioritize domain expertise, problem-solving ability, and system design skills over specific language proficiency. A senior developer with deep e-commerce domain knowledge but limited experience in Go can be productive in a Go codebase from day one with AI assistance.

The Future — Will Programming Languages Still Matter?

This is the question that every developer is asking. If AI coding agents can handle syntax and standard patterns across all languages, does it still matter which language you use?

The answer is nuanced. Programming languages will still matter, but for different reasons than they do today. Languages will be chosen for their performance characteristics, ecosystem quality, safety guarantees, and community support — not for the availability of developers who know them.

Rust will be chosen for memory safety and performance, not because it is hard to find Rust developers. Go will be chosen for its simplicity and fast compilation, not because the team already knows Go. Python will be chosen for its ecosystem and readability, not because it is easy to learn.

The languages themselves will also evolve. As AI coding agents become the primary interface for writing code, language design may shift toward patterns that AI tools handle well. We may see languages optimized for AI-assisted development, with clearer semantics, better type systems, and more predictable patterns.

Conclusion — Embracing the Multi-Language Future

AI coding agents are removing programming language barriers, and this is fundamentally changing how software is built. The era of the language-specific developer is ending. In its place, we are entering an era of the AI-assisted polyglot developer — someone who can work across any language, any framework, and any codebase with the help of intelligent coding agents.

The key to success in this new era is not to resist the change but to embrace it. Developers should invest in problem-solving skills, system design knowledge, and domain expertise — the areas where human judgment remains irreplaceable. Companies should rethink their hiring practices, onboarding processes, and technology choices to take advantage of the expanded possibilities that AI coding agents enable.

The programming language barrier that once defined the boundaries of a developer’s career is dissolving. The question is no longer “what languages do you know?” but “what can you build?”

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can AI coding agents completely replace the need to learn programming languages? A: No. AI coding agents handle syntax and standard patterns, but developers still need to understand programming concepts, evaluate AI output critically, and make architectural decisions. The goal is not to skip learning but to learn more efficiently by building real projects with AI assistance.

Q: Which AI coding agent is best for cross-language development? A: The best tool depends on your workflow. Cursor excels as an AI-native IDE with deep codebase understanding. Claude Code is ideal for terminal-based developers who need autonomous multi-file operations. GitHub Copilot offers the broadest integration with the GitHub ecosystem and the largest user community.

Q: Is AI-generated code in unfamiliar languages safe for production? A: AI-generated code should always be reviewed by a human with appropriate expertise. While AI coding agents produce syntactically correct code, they can introduce subtle bugs, security vulnerabilities, or performance issues that require human judgment to catch.

Q: How long does it take to become productive in a new language with AI coding agents? A: Multiple developer reports, including the Rails at Scale case study, indicate that developers can contribute meaningfully to projects in unfamiliar languages from day one when using AI coding agents. Full proficiency still develops over time through continued practice and learning.

Q: Will AI coding agents make programming language expertise obsolete? A: No. Deep language expertise will remain valuable for performance optimization, debugging complex issues, and making architectural decisions. However, the barrier to working across multiple languages is significantly lower, making polyglot development accessible to all developers rather than just specialists.

item.title: The AI Coding Tool You Use Is Now a Hiring Signal: Developer Career Guide (2026)
item.description: The AI coding tool you use is now a hiring signal. Here's how employers evaluate AI proficiency, which tools to put on your resume, and how to navigate the new developer job market in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
Why Your AI Coding Tool Choice Matters for Your Career

I’ve been watching hiring patterns shift over the past 18 months, and one thing is clear: the AI coding tool you use has become a career signal whether you like it or not.

In 2024, listing “Copilot” on your resume was a curiosity. In 2025, it was table stakes. In 2026, hiring managers are actively screening for which tools you use and how you use them. The Stack Overflow 2025 survey reported that 84% of developers use AI coding tools, with 47.1% using them daily. When nearly half the industry uses these tools every single day, the question is no longer “Do you use AI?” — it’s “Which tools do you use, and are you any good with them?”

This isn’t a hype take. I’ve seen job descriptions that explicitly ask for “experience with Claude Code, Cursor, or equivalent AI coding agents.” I’ve talked to hiring managers who filter candidates based on whether they can articulate a coherent AI-assisted workflow. And I’ve watched the junior market get squeezed in ways that should concern every developer early in their career.

Let me walk through what’s actually happening, what the data says, and how you should think about your own career strategy.

The New Hiring Signal: How Employers Evaluate AI Tool Proficiency

Here’s the uncomfortable truth: AI tools make it easier to fake competence on a resume. A candidate can generate a polished GitHub profile, produce clean-looking PRs, and ace a take-home assignment — all with AI assistance. Hiring managers know this. So they’ve adapted.

The new screening criteria I’m seeing in 2026 fall into three buckets:

1. Tool-specific experience. Employers want to know if you’ve used Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, or Codex CLI — and they’re starting to care about the distinction. A candidate who’s only used Copilot autocomplete is viewed differently from someone who’s built agentic workflows with Claude Code. The $3B acquisition of Windsurf by OpenAI in 2025 signaled that these tools are strategic assets, not toys.

2. Workflow articulation. Can you describe how you use AI in your daily work? “I use Copilot for autocomplete” is a weak signal. “I use Claude Code with a custom AGENTS.md for project context, run plan mode before implementing, and use code review agents for PR quality” is a strong one. Hiring managers want to see that you’ve developed a methodology, not just a habit.

3. Quality judgment. The most valuable skill in the AI era is knowing when not to trust AI output. Candidates who can articulate their verification strategy — how they test, review, and validate AI-generated code — stand out. This is the difference between someone who ships garbage faster and someone who ships quality faster.

The State of AI Coding Tools in 2026 — Market Overview

The AI coding tool market has consolidated into clear tiers. I covered the broader landscape in my State of AI Coding Agents 2026 post, but here’s what the hiring-relevant landscape looks like right now:

Agentic CLI tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI) — These run in your terminal, can edit files, run commands, and manage multi-step workflows. Claude Code has become the de facto standard for serious agentic development, with a rich ecosystem of hooks, subagents, and plan modes.

IDE-integrated agents (Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot) — These live inside your editor. Cursor and Windsurf have been battling for the “AI-native IDE” crown, with Windsurf’s Arena Mode and Cursor’s agent features pushing each other forward. Copilot remains the most widely deployed but is playing catch-up on agentic features.

Specialized platforms (Devin, Factory, SWE-Agent) — These are more autonomous, handling entire tickets or PRs. They’re less relevant for individual developer resumes but signal the direction of the industry.

The key insight: tool choice signals developer philosophy. Someone who uses Claude Code with strict plan mode and code review hooks is signaling they value control and quality. Someone who uses Cursor with Composer is signaling they value tight IDE integration. Someone who only uses Copilot autocomplete is signaling… well, that they haven’t explored much.

Which AI Coding Tools Should You Put on Your Resume?

Not all AI tool experience is created equal. Here’s my honest take on what’s worth listing and what’s not:

Definitely list:

  • Claude Code — The strongest signal in 2026. It shows you work with agentic, terminal-based tools and can handle complex multi-file workflows. Mention specific features you use: plan mode, subagents, hooks, MCP servers.
  • Cursor — Strong signal, especially if you use its agent and Composer features. Mention how you’ve configured rules, used context management, or integrated with your team’s workflow.
  • Windsurf — Good signal, especially post-acquisition. Arena Mode and Cascade are worth calling out specifically.
  • Codex CLI / Gemini CLI — Niche but respected. Shows you’re exploring the cutting edge.

Maybe list (with context):

  • GitHub Copilot — Table stakes. Everyone has used it. If you list it, pair it with something more specific: “Copilot for autocomplete, Claude Code for complex refactoring.”
  • Devin / Factory — Only if you’ve actually used them in a production context, not just tried the demo.

Don’t bother listing:

  • Generic “AI coding tools” — Too vague. It signals you don’t know what you’re talking about.
  • ChatGPT for coding — Everyone uses it. It’s like listing “Google Search” on your resume.

The rule: list tools where you can speak to specific workflows, trade-offs, and outcomes. If you can’t describe how you’d set up a project with that tool, don’t put it on your resume.

How to Demonstrate Genuine AI Coding Proficiency

Casual use and genuine proficiency look different. I wrote about this distinction in detail in Vibe Coding vs Agentic Engineering, but here’s the hiring-relevant summary of what separates them:

Casual use: You open ChatGPT, paste an error, copy the fix. You use Copilot tab-complete for boilerplate. You’ve tried Cursor once.

Genuine proficiency: You have a repeatable workflow. You know which tasks to delegate to AI and which to handle yourself. You can debug when the AI produces wrong output. You’ve built custom configurations — AGENTS.md files, custom instructions, MCP server integrations.
